prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots place B019 first, but unanimity of ranking is not itself the argument. The scientific case is that it is one of the few discovery chains in modern medicine that runs unbroken from hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its insulinotropic and satiety actions) to therapies with independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Mechanism and clinical benefit are confirmed in many large randomised trials and years of global use, so maturity is not a concern and recognition is timely. I would frame the citation around the physiology and the active peptide, which keeps the prize in the discovery domain and gives a coherent three-person set of Holst, Drucker and Mojsov.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and the three-person limit forces an exclusion. Knudsen's long-acting acylated analogues are what turned the biology into liraglutide and semaglutide, and without them the physiology would not have reached patients at this scale; Habener, who is not in the supplied credit list, is also relevant to the peptide history. A physiology-only prize can be read as under-crediting the step that created the drugs, while a prize that includes drug development blurs the line between discovery and industrial optimisation. The Mojsov priority question is sensitive and I cannot adjudicate it from the supplied materials.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the prize should follow the path from basic hormone biology to durable receptor agonists and that Mojsov's role is real but harder to place.
responses.response: I take the point that the drugs are the reason this prize is urgent, and I do not dismiss Knudsen. But I disagree with replacing Mojsov. Identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is the discovery step that made both the physiology and the pharmacology tractable, whereas analogue design is optimisation of a known peptide within a company programme. Excluding the person who defined the active molecule in favour of the person who extended its half-life would invert the usual hierarchy between discovery and development. If the committee wants to credit the drugs, I would rather see that argued explicitly than reached indirectly through the choice of names.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks TOR signalling third and proposes Michael Hall alone, on the grounds that identification of TOR in yeast is the decisive foundational step and that the later mTOR complex credit is unsettled.
responses.response: A single-laureate TOR prize is the cleanest reading of the foundational step, and I agree that Hall's genetic identification is what the field rests on. My reservation is about distinctiveness and medical consequence rather than credit: the clinical output of rapalogs has been narrower than the biology suggested, and I rank it sixth, below the unfolded protein response, which I find the more conceptually self-contained discovery. I would not oppose Hall alone if the committee gets there, but I would not exclude Schreiber's chemical genetics on the strength of conduct questions about Sabatini, which concern a different person and which I cannot verify.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks CAR-T second and weighs June and Sadelain most heavily, while placing TNF blockade for rheumatoid arthritis third as a clear concept chain with a natural two-person allocation.
responses.response: I agree that June and Sadelain carry the decisive design and translational contribution in CAR-T, which is why I proposed only the two of them. I disagree with adding Rosenberg: adoptive cell transfer is a framework that preceded CAR design, and including him widens the award beyond the discovery the ballot names. On TNF blockade I would qualify the support. The Feldmann and Maini chain is strong and mature, but no other member ranked it, and I would want to understand why before treating it as a competitor to CAR-T.

responses.point: El Manira ranks optogenetics second as a method of exceptional originality and breadth that has transformed circuit analysis, including motor and spinal circuits.
responses.response: I share the view that optogenetics is among the most influential methods in neuroscience, and as a neurologist I see its first clinical use in vision restoration. But I ranked it fourth because the question is whether a tool fits the prize now, and six credible names with at most three slots makes any configuration contestable. Impact on research is not the same as a discovery in physiology or medicine, and I would want the committee to settle the Bamberg and Boyden exclusion before I move it up. It remains a serious candidate, but it is not strong enough to displace the GLP-1 prize this year.

uncertainties: Priority and credit among Mojsov, Habener, Holst and Drucker cannot be resolved from the supplied materials, and Habener is outside the credit list.
Whether the committee wants the citation to cover only physiology and the active peptide or also the drug development represented by Knudsen.
Whether the unfolded protein response or CAR-T is the stronger second candidate if the committee prefers a two-part prize, since the three-person limit would then force a split of the GLP-1 names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Thomas Perlmann and worked with Paul Greengard, but neither relationship bears on any shortlisted ballot or credited name. I have not inferred ties from shared institutions or topics.
